newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil vote-buying deputies skirt impeachment.
newsitem.headline: Brazil vote-buying deputies skirt impeachment.

text.p: Two Brazilian deputies implicated in an alleged money-for-votes scandal resigned from Congress on Wednesday, just hours before a congressional investigation was expected to recommend their impeachment, officials said.

Chamber of Deputies members Ronivon Santiago and Joao Maia, both from the Amazonian frontier state of Acre, said in their resignation letters they were standing down for "personal reasons," an official in the office of lower house president Michel Temer said.
"They've resigned, citing personal reasons," the official, who asked not to be identified, said.

Santiago and Maia were among five deputies from Acre suspected of having accepted $190,000 from the governors of Acre and Amazonas states for voting in favour of a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to seek re-election.
The deputies have denied the allegations and Cardoso, keeping an extremely low profile to distance himself from the claims, has also rejected charges of wrongdoing.

The alleged vote-buying scam came to light last week when tapes of Santiago and Maia talking to a mysterious "Mr X" were published by the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper. The news rocked the government and dealt a serious blow to investor confidence.
Both deputies weer kicked out of their party, the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL).

An internal congressional investigation was due to conclude its investigation on Wednesday after receiving a report from forensic scientists of the University of Campinas in Sao Paulo state. The scientists verified the authenticity of the tapes and identified the voices of Santiago and Maia, officials said.
As a result, the congressional investigators were expected to recommend the impeachment of the deputies, disqualifying them from seeking public office for eight years.
But their resignation scuppered that option.
"Clearly it will no longer be possible to impeach the deputies because they are no longer deputies," the lower house presidency official said.
The money-for-votes scandal has hit President Cardoso at a sensitive time.

His government is trying to push through essential fiscal reforms in Congress and the re-election bill has to pass twice through the Senate, the first of those votes scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.

The re-election law, which would allow sitting presidents, governors and mayors to stand for a second term for the first time since the republic was founded in 1889, was approved by the Chamber of Deputies in January.
A poll due to be published on Thursday but anticipated by the Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper on Tuesday showed Cardoso's approval rating had plummeted 20 points to 50 percent since March.
